artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the set of all finite words over $A$. Given a (possibly infinite, but recursively presented) set of words $F \subseteq A^*$, an $F$-factorization of a word $w \in A^*$ is a sequence of words $u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_k \in F$ such that $w = u_1 u_2 \cdots u_k$. Several decision and enumeration problems are naturally associated with $F$-factorizations, for instance:

(i) Existence: given $w$, decide whether $w$ admits an $F$-factorization.
(ii) Counting: given $w$, compute the number of distinct $F$-factorizations of $w$.
(iii) Optimization: given $w$, find an $F$-factorization minimizing or maximizing the number of factors.
(iv) Uniqueness: decide whether every word over $A$ has at most one $F$-factorization (i.e., whether $F$ is a code).

For natural classes of sets $F$ (such as regular sets, sets defined by avoidance of a finite list of patterns, sets of bifix-free or unbordered words, sets of Lyndon words, etc.) several of the above problems are known to be solvable in polynomial time in $|w|$, but the exponents and constants of the known algorithms are often far from optimal.

Problem. For each of the $F$-factorization problems above that is known to be solvable in polynomial time, design an algorithm whose running time is as efficient as possible — ideally linear or quasi-linear in the length of the input word $w$ — and establish matching lower bounds in a suitable model of computation.
artifact.status_search_result: No specific resolution of this open-ended algorithmic question on F-factorizations of words was located. The problem is broad (asking for improved algorithms across several polynomial-time-solvable F-factorization problems), and progress on individual subproblems exists in the combinatorics-on-words literature, but no comprehensive solution was found.
